full_judgment: 23. This line of reasoning deems to be quit logical. We need not, however, express any final opinion in this regard, as the decision in this case may be more appropriately founded on a different premise. It appears no doubt from the provision of Order 41, rule 1(1) that the requirement that the Memorandum shall be accompanied by a copy of the decree appealed from is compulsory Under the provision of the said rule the Court has power to dispense with the filing of a copy of the judgment but not of the decree, for the obvious reason that according to the provision of the Code as contained in section 96, it is against a decree that an appeal lies. When a suit has been disposed of by a judgment, a decree shall follow in accordance with the provision of section 33 of the Code and a formal decree is prepared in accordance with the provision of rules 6-19 of Order 20 of the Code. The case of an appeal against an order rejecting the plaint under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code stands, however, on a different footing. Such an order which may be made even before the appearance of a defendant is not strictly an adjudication in respect of any of the rights in controversy between the parties and does not come within the substantive provision of the definition clause as incorporated in section 2(2) of the Code, but it is a decree in view of the inclusive provision of the definition clause, which provides that the expression, 'decree', "shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within section 47 or section 144." The provisions of Order 20 of the Code which lay down procedural rules relating to pronouncement and signing of a judgment and the drawing up of a decree which is to follow such a judgment do not strictly appear to have any application to such an order as is itself deemed to be a decree under the definition clause.
